chapter_theme: The king rides out to the spring groves, which flatter his women and are drawn as copies of their bodies, then goes to the shrine of the Arhat where he and the descending charanas sing hymns of a god who needs no praise and is loved all the same.

cast.role: the king who goes to the spring groves, then to the shrine
heavenly sages who descend and sing to the Arhat
the Arhat worshipped in the shrine and in the charanas' song

167.reading: Girls at doll-play, already touched by love's god, fear he will take their lives and leave; they carry their parrots and mynas and wail through all the groves.
167.nuance: The syntax of lines 1 to 3 is compressed in the edition's word division; the sense of the girls' fear is held with some doubt.

168.reading: Told of spring, the king leaves the city with his children, his household and the keepers of his household, riding elephant and chariot, and comes to the pleasure groves.
168.nuance: The first line's வயந்தம் may be spring personified as the announcer; the edition's division leaves this open.
168.event: The king sets out from the city with his children and retinue for the spring groves.

169.reading: As the king arrives, the groves greet him: flowers scatter, koel birds sing a blessing, and slender creepers lift their buds in salutation like women who speak good omens.

170.reading: The woodland honours him further: creepers pour pollen as scented powder, boughs wave like fly-whisks, and the kongu buds open as umbrellas.

171.reading: Bees hum like bards singing his virtue, and parrots shake down cool flowers as though strewing the tokens of homage before the spear-bearing lord.

172.reading: A breeze bathes in the creepers' honey and the stream, sets the bees singing, and loosens flowers on the king's crown.

173.reading: With spring thus welcoming him, the king of the earth takes pleasure in showing his women the groves and bids them play till their waists ache.
173.nuance: The poet names him with the sceptre (செங்கோன்) in passing; the verse makes no claim about justice and links no sceptre to the play.
173.event: The king shows the groves to his women and bids them play.

174.reading: The mango and the flaming ashoka, the punnai with its scattered pollen, and the bee-hummed banks show spring shining like the wealth of the women addressed.
174.nuance: The comparison of spring's bloom to the women's wealth (செல்வம்) turns the scene's praise toward the women, not the season.

175.reading: The shoots of the ashoka and the young creepers are said to have taken their forms from the women's hands and waists, so nature is made to borrow from the body.

176.reading: Mango shoots take the women's colour, koels learn their speech, and flowering trees gather their lips' red: spring is drawn as a copy of women.

177.reading: Lotus and water-lily ponds and pavilions would dazzle even the love-god, but women without mates, with sweet parrot speech, will hardly live through this spring.
177.nuance: The verse turns the season's beauty into a danger for the unpartnered, as the Kural's love chapters do for the parted.

178.reading: Having thus delighted the young women, the king takes leave of the spring, and goes with flowers to the golden city of the temple shrine.
178.nuance: மன்னவன் வயந்தமாட் டருளி is difficult; the sense of taking leave of spring is a reading, not fixed.
178.event: The king leaves the spring grove and goes to the city where the god's shrine stands.

179.reading: Glad, the king walks round the shrine of the clan's god from right to left, and its gem-set doors burst open with bright light.
179.event: The king circles the shrine and its jewelled doors open.

180.reading: The shrine of the god of unmeasured might shines: it is said to drive out ills, end births, and give boons to heaven.
180.nuance: The verse credits the shrine and its god with ending births (பிறவி தீர்ப்பன) without saying whose own effort does it; Jain doctrine elsewhere leaves release to the self's own work.

claims.claim: the shrine of the Arhat removes ills, ends births and gives boons

181.reading: The king, with hair standing on end and radiant, joins his hands and praises well the red lotus feet of him who conquered the harsh dust of karma.
181.event: The king bows in worship before the conqueror of karma.

claims.claim: the one worthy of praise is he who has conquered the karma that torments

182.reading: They say the god of pure body and bright limbs is called the knower of all; yet even called so, the world-holder is hard to truly know.
182.nuance: The refrain repeats the line, an old pattern of hymn that turns each epithet back on itself; the claim is about the limits of naming.

claims.claim: the Arhat is omniscient but cannot be fully known even by one who names him so

183.reading: They say the god who has no bird-borne weapon and has conquered all strife is the Lord; yet even so named, he is hard to know.
183.nuance: The unarmed god may be set against gods who bear weapons; the verse does not name any rival.

claims.claim: the Arhat has conquered strife and carries no weapon, but even so he is hard to know

184.reading: They say the god with the auspicious mark on his right is without any blemish; even so told, the one who unfolded the great scripture is hard to know.

claims.claim: the Arhat is without blemish and is the source of the scripture

185.reading: Having praised the Lord thus, the king bows his head with the flower of the offering, shuts the gem doors, and walks to the courtyard of his shining palace.
185.event: The king ends his worship, closes the shrine doors and goes to his palace courtyard.

186.reading: The charanas, heavenly sages, come down from the sky as the scripture's flame burns, circle the father's rich city and bless him with bells ringing.
186.event: The charanas descend and circle the city, singing.

187.reading: Their song addresses the one who walked above a lotus, saying that though he is not pleased by their praise, they will not give up love for him who stood so that all the world rejoiced.
187.nuance: The pattern repeats in 187 to 189; each time the praise concedes that he feels no delight, then keeps the love anyway.
187.event: The charanas sing to the Arhat.

claims.claim: the Arhat is untouched by praise, yet merits love for the joy he brought the world

188.reading: They say again that though he does not take joy in being worshipped beside the lotus, they will not give up love for him who stood in a state that cannot be reversed, so the path rejoices.

claims.claim: the Arhat takes no joy in worship, yet his unreturning state earns love

189.reading: They say a third time that he is not glad when the heavens bow and they praise, yet the cool world rejoices at his standing, so they will not leave their love.

claims.claim: the Arhat takes no joy in praise, yet the world rejoices in him

190.reading: The sweet song of the lovers of the sage's lord ends, and all lives that heard it were freed from sorrow, as long as it lasted.
190.nuance: The poet closes the hymn with the claim that hearing it soothes lives; the bound of the verse's last two lines is hard to fix.

links.note: Verse 187 hails the god as walking above the lotus, as Kural 3 speaks of the one who walked upon the flower.
links.teaches: The same lotus-walker of the opening couplet appears here as an epic's praised Arhat, so the image carries a Jain form where the Kural leaves the Lord unnamed.

gains.a: The lotus-walker is given an addressee, a congregation that loves him though he feels no pleasure, which the verse's own words alone do not show for any named god.
gains.b: A worship scene in which the image sits within a story of devotees, where the couplet states it as a bare mark.

links.note: Verse 188 says the god takes no joy in praise yet is loved; Kural 4 says the god without liking or aversion frees those who reach his feet.
links.teaches: The epic turns the Kural's rule of the one without liking into a devotional posture: love offered without any hope of being pleased.

gains.a: A reason why the worshippers do not need his pleasure, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: A scene of worship that tests the claim that the one without liking cannot be moved by praise.

links.note: Verse 182 says even calling the Arhat all-knowing does not let one know him; Tirumanthiram 32 says no one knows the lord's nature, and the all-pervading lord is praised only in part.
links.teaches: Both say naming does not reach the god, but the Jain verse accepts omniscience as a true name while the Saiva verse denies any measure of the lord.

gains.a: The verse's refusal is made sharper: it concedes the epithet and still holds the god beyond it, where the Saiva line denies all naming.
gains.b: A rival that praises by listing epithets, so the lord beyond naming can be seen as a stand against it.

links.note: Verse 175 draws spring shoots as copies of the women's hands and waists; Naladiyar 48 tells those who praise sandal and garland without knowing the body to look at vultures tearing the carcass.
links.teaches: A court poet delights in the body's beauty while a moral quatrain holds the same body as carrion, so the same poem tradition holds two views of the body.

gains.a: A counter-voice that sees the beauty it praises as fading.
gains.b: A quatrain's image set against a living scene of pleasure, so its rebuke has a concrete target.

links.note: Verse 180 says the shrine and its god end births; Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
links.teaches: The epic locates the ending of births in the shrine and its god, where the Kural puts it in the devotee's reaching.

gains.a: A statement of what the god gives, not only what the devotee reaches.
gains.b: A place in which the reaching happens, the shrine.

links.note: Verse 181 praises him who conquered the harsh dust of karma; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
links.teaches: The epic names the conqueror of karma whose praise the Kural says keeps deed from clinging, so it names the one the couplet leaves as 'the Lord'.

gains.a: A Lord defined by his conquest of karma, so what the praise protects against is plain.
gains.b: A reader's reason why praise should loosen the deeds' hold.

links.note: Verse 179 opens the shrine's gem doors at the king's coming; verse 185 shuts them after his praise.
links.teaches: The worship is bounded by an opening and a closing of the doors, so the whole of the praise lies between them.

source_issues: Verses 168, 178: the word வயந்தம் and the phrase வயந்தமாட்டருளி are hard to construe from the edition's word division; flagged uncertain.
Verse 174 line 3: 'வரியணி ந்து' has a stray space in the edition.
